content.title: 6.5. Antiplatelet therapy in patients requiring oral anticoagulation
content.section: 6.5.1. Acute coronary syndrome patients requiring anticoagulation
content.summary: A minority (approximately 6–8%) of patients undergoing PCI require long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC). Long-term OAC should be continued during the invasive procedure; interruption and bridging may increase thrombo-embolic events and bleeding. It is uncertain whether to bridge non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOACs) with parenteral anticoagulants or to continue NOACs without additional parenteral anticoagulation. In patients treated with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), no parenteral anticoagulation is needed if the international normalized ratio (INR) is >2.5.
content.table7_title: Suggested strategies to reduce bleeding risk related to percutaneous coronary intervention
suggested_strategies: Adjust anticoagulant doses to body weight and renal function, especially in women and older patients
Use radial artery approach as default vascular access
Use proton pump inhibitors in patients on dual antiplatelet therapy who are at higher-than-average risk of gastrointestinal bleeds
content.proton_pump_inhibitor_criteria: Consider PPI if history of GI ulcer/haemorrhage, on anticoagulant therapy, chronic NSAID/corticosteroid use, OR presence of two or more listed risk factors
in_patients_on_OAC: Perform PCI without interruption of VKAs or NOACs where appropriate
In patients on VKAs, do not administer unfractionated heparin (UFH) if INR > 2.5
practice_notes: Interruption of long-term OAC and bridging with parenteral anticoagulants may lead to increased thrombo-embolic episodes and bleeds
Uncertainty exists about safest approach for NOACs during PCI (bridging vs continuation without parenteral anticoagulation)
